# Acta for coding agents

Describes Acta 1.0.0-rc.11: the packages Acta.Sqlite, Acta.Postgres, Acta.SqlServer, Acta.Dashboard, and
Acta.AspNetCore at that version. Verified 2026-11-14. When this file and an installed package disagree, the
package wins: the compiler and `<app> jobs help` outrank this file. In an existing app, read its resolved Acta
version first and follow the docs at that tag, github.com/acta-dotnet/acta/tree/v<version>; do not upgrade
the app to match an example.

Acta is a durable job and workflow engine for .NET backed by the application's own SQL database
(PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or embedded SQLite). One handler can record steps and variables, start
child jobs and fan out with Map, Parallel, and Join, and wait for signals and timers without
holding a worker; lanes keep per-entity order, and concurrency and rate limits hold across every
worker. Jobs, schedules, steps, waits, and alerts are ordinary rows. This file is the contract an agent needs to add Acta to a project correctly; the
runnable proof lives in the repository's `concepts/` directory (compiled, one project per concept) and the
complete demo apps under `demos/`. Start at useacta.net or github.com/acta-dotnet/acta.

## The one rule everything follows from

Execution is at-least-once, and a handler re-enters from the top. After a crash, a lease expiry, a
retry, or a resumed wait, Acta runs the handler method again from its first line. Completed steps,
variables, timers, and signal waits return their recorded results instead of repeating
their work; every bare line between them runs again on every entry. The model is checkpoints, not
replay: there is no determinism requirement on your code, and there is no magic resume-at-line-N.

Those recorded results and the ledger make re-entry something you can reason about and test, because
everything a handler decided is a row you can read. Write handlers as if the method will be
called twice with the same input, and put every external side effect behind a step.

## First run: one file, one job, the dashboard

```bash
dotnet new web -n Shipping && cd Shipping
dotnet add package Acta.Sqlite --prerelease
dotnet add package Acta.Dashboard --prerelease
```

Replace `Program.cs` with this, all of it:

```csharp
using Shipping;                 // the generated manifest lands in your project's root namespace
using Acta;
using Acta.Dashboard;
using Acta.Sqlite;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.UseActa(j =>
{
    j.UseSqlite(sqlite =>
    {
        sqlite.ConnectionString = "Data Source=acta-local.db";
        sqlite.MigrateOnStartup = true;   // local development only; in production a deploy step runs "jobs migrate"
    });
    j.Run<ShippingJobs>("shipping");
});

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapActa("/acta");           // dashboard + JSON API; local-only by default, controls disabled

// Your own endpoint enqueues: the job is a durable row before the response goes out.
app.MapPost("/orders/{orderId:int}", async (int orderId, IJobs jobs) =>
{
    var job = await jobs.EnqueueAsync(new ShipOrder(orderId));
    return Results.Accepted("/acta", new { job.JobRef });
});

app.Run();

public sealed record ShipOrder(int OrderId);

public static class ShippingHandlers
{
    [Job("ship-order")]
    public static void Handle(ShipOrder input) => Console.WriteLine($"Shipping order {input.OrderId}");
}
```

`dotnet run`, then `curl -X POST http://localhost:<port>/orders/1042` on the port it printed: the app prints
`Shipping order 1042` and the dashboard lists the job. Rules this sample carries:

- `[Job("ship-order")]` is required and a name: dotted kebab-case, `[a-z][a-z0-9-]*` segments joined by `.`
  (`billing.send-invoice`), no underscores, no trailing dash, at most 128 chars. The bare `sys` and the `sys.` prefix are reserved for Acta's own jobs. The name is
  the durable operator-facing contract in SQL, the dashboard, the CLI, and alerts.
- `ShippingJobs` is the source-generated manifest, named from the LAST segment of the project's
  `RootNamespace` plus `Jobs` (`Users` → `UsersJobs`; a segment already ending in `Jobs` gets
  `Manifest` instead: `TestJobs` → `TestJobsManifest`). It is generated into that root namespace,
  so a `Program.cs` with a top-level namespace needs `using Shipping;` to see it.
- Enqueue is type-driven: the input record's type routes the call, one `EnqueueAsync` for every
  job. It answers a `JobHandle`: `await job.WaitAsync()` follows the job to its outcome without stopping it.
  `ScheduleAsync(input, TimeSpan)` or `ScheduleAsync(input, DateTimeOffset)` runs one job later; a recurring
  schedule is `[Schedule]`. The host that enqueues can also execute; there is no separate worker process
  unless you want one.
- A schedule's instants come from a cron, an interval, or a calendar bound by name (`Calendar = "pay-days"`),
  and any schedule fires only inside an availability calendar's windows when it names one
  (`Availability = "office-hours"`). A name is a catalog family, defined as JSON and published through
  `IActaOperations.Calendars`, the HTTP API, or the dashboard's Calendars page, in the namespace or shared in `sys`.
  Publish it before the deploy of the jobs that name it: a deploy whose schedule names a calendar with no
  published version fails and writes nothing. The page is `docs/scheduling.md`.
- Each job's member on `ShippingJobs` is a factory taking the handler's input parameters and returning the
  job's call: `jobs.EnqueueAsync(ShippingJobs.ShipOrder(new ShipOrder(orderId)))` names the job outright, and a
  result job's call answers `JobHandle<TResult>`. An enqueue that reads no result can pass the input alone, options
  included: `jobs.EnqueueAsync(new ShipOrder(orderId), o => o.DeduplicationKey(key))`. A handler may take several input parameters before `JobContext` and
  `CancellationToken`; they travel as one generated record, `ShippingJobs.{Job}Args`, whose parameter names
  are stored JSON keys. Under Native AOT, declare the input record yourself and take it as the one parameter.
- The handle follows the job without another lookup: `await handle.WaitAsync()` answers its outcome, `await handle.GetResultAsync()` returns the stored result
  and throws when there is none, and `await handle.TryGetResultAsync()` answers `(Found, Value)` for a result that may not exist yet.
  From a ref the same reads are on `IJobs`: `jobs.GetResultAsync<ShipmentLabel>(jobRef)`. Neither read waits.
- An `IJobs` call that addresses a job takes a `JobLookup`, and both the handle an enqueue answered and a `JobRef` convert to one, so pass what you hold: `jobs.GetStatusAsync(jobRef)`. A ref that arrives as text, from a route or a column of your own, is `JobRef.Parse(text)` or `JobRef.TryParse`. `JobLookup.ByDeduplicationKey(jobNamespace, key)` finds the job a key made.
- Handlers resolve through DI: an instance class's constructor dependencies must be registered. One DI cannot build fails its job on the first attempt with `HandlerActivationException`, never retried, and the message names the missing service.

## Wiring rules by situation

- New app: ASP.NET Core empty host + `Acta.Sqlite` + `Acta.Dashboard` with `MapActa("/acta")` and
  one real job, exactly as above.
- Existing app: inspect its hosting and database first and preserve both. Add the matching
  provider package (`Acta.Postgres` / `Acta.SqlServer` / `Acta.Sqlite`) and register with the
  existing connection string; do not change the host type to add Acta.
- Producer and worker in the same assembly: typed `EnqueueAsync` plus `j.Run<TManifest>(...)`, as
  above. This is the default.
- Split deployment (API enqueues, separate worker executes): the worker registers
  `Run<TManifest>`; the producer enqueues by the raw route contract instead of the typed call so
  it does not need the handler assembly.
- Never enable `MigrateOnStartup` outside an explicitly local or development configuration. There, startup applies the schema and writes the app's jobs and schedules, so one `dotnet run` is enough.
- Production runs `<app> jobs migrate` from a deploy step before the new build starts: it applies the schema, deploys the app's job definitions and schedules, and records the app's version. `<app> jobs deploy` does the deploy alone and needs no DDL right. A worker start writes no definition or schedule, and refuses a namespace its build's version has not deployed in.
- Once `jobs migrate` or `jobs deploy` has deployed a namespace, a `MigrateOnStartup` start writes no definition or schedule there, on a local database too: a new or changed job then takes `jobs deploy`, or a fresh local database.
- Give each build its own version: `JobsOptions.DeploymentVersion`, by default the entry assembly's informational version. An app that is `1.0.0` on every build is one version to Acta.
- An external outbox table comes from the producer's own migrations (`CreateOutboxScript()`) or `ApplyOutboxAsync`; Acta never creates it on its own.
- Rolling deploys are routine: run `<app> jobs migrate`, start the new build, stop the old one, with any overlap. Acta's migrations are forward-only and keep an old and a new build working on one schema; a worker hands back a job whose handler it lacks and stops claiming that definition; a deploy never retires a definition the new build omits, so a rollback keeps the queue. What the application keeps is its own, as in any rolling deploy: a queued input the new build still reads, and a step name a running job still finds. Retiring a dropped definition and cancelling its queue is an operator action on the definition.
- Definitions and schedules are the current deployment's. An older build's workers write nothing, and its `jobs deploy` changes nothing unless run with `--force`, which is how a rollback restores the earlier definitions. A schedule a deploy drops is orphaned and loses its pause, so to hold a permanent job across a rollback, pause the job, not the schedule.

## Steps

`await ctx.RunStepAsync("name", ct => ...)` is a named run-once step. On re-entry a completed step
returns its recorded result instead of running the body. That promise has two conditions:

- The outcome is durable only after it is recorded. A crash after the side effect ran but before
  the outcome landed re-runs the body on replay, so the body must be idempotent, usually via a
  stable key derived from the job, never from the attempt.
- Only step-wrapped work is skipped. Bare handler code between steps re-runs on every entry.

A step retries through its job: a body that throws fails the attempt, the job's `MaxAttempts` and
`Backoff` retry it, and the retry replays the steps that succeeded and runs this one again. A wait
inside a step body works: the resume runs the body up to the wait, which returns what it has, and
charges nothing.

To compensate before the last failure lands, catch on `ctx.IsLastAttempt`, which reads the budget the
job has already spent (and a Strict deadline), never the execution number:
`catch (Exception ex) when (ctx.IsLastAttempt || ex is StepFailedException) { await ctx.RunStepAsync("release-stock", ...); throw; }`.
The filter takes `StepFailedException` too because a non-retryable exception ends the job on any
attempt. That is best effort: a crash or a lost lease on the last attempt skips the catch, so the compensation
is an idempotent step, and work whose compensation must happen runs as a child job the parent
compensates when the child lands `Failed`.

For side effects where a duplicate is worse than an ambiguous interruption (a payment capture),
`AtMostOnce()` runs the body zero-or-one times and hands the handler an explicit interrupted state to
reconcile. A body that throws fails the step for good: every later attempt throws `StepFailedException`
for it without running the body, so left uncaught it fails the job at once; catch it where the job can
go on, and an operator restart runs the step again. A wait inside an at-most-once body throws at the
call, because its resume would run the body again.

## An external side effect, done right

```csharp
using Acta;

namespace Shipping;

public sealed record DeliverWebhook(Guid DeliveryId, string Url, string Payload);

public sealed class WebhookJobs(HttpClient http)
{
    [Job("deliver-webhook", MaxAttempts = 5)]
    public async Task Handle(DeliverWebhook input, JobContext ctx, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // The idempotency key comes from the JOB (stable across attempts), never the attempt.
        var signature = await ctx.RunStepAsync("sign-payload",
            _ => Task.FromResult($"{input.DeliveryId}:{input.Payload.Length}"), ct);

        var status = await ctx.RunStepAsync("post", async token =>
        {
            using var request = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post, input.Url);
            request.Headers.Add("Idempotency-Key", input.DeliveryId.ToString());
            request.Headers.Add("X-Signature", signature);
            request.Content = new StringContent(input.Payload);
            using var response = await http.SendAsync(request, token);
            // A failed delivery throws, so the step records no success and the attempt retries; which
            // statuses deserve a retry is this application's call, not a framework policy.
            response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
            return (int)response.StatusCode;
        }, ct);

        await ctx.RunStepAsync("record-response",
            _ => Task.FromResult(status), ct);
    }
}
```

Register `HttpClient` in DI (`builder.Services.AddHttpClient<WebhookJobs>();`). A step that recorded
its outcome is reused on re-entry, so a crash after `post` recorded its status never sends again;
`record-response` replays from the row. The window for a duplicate is narrower: the receiver accepted
the request, then the process died before Acta recorded the `post` outcome. The retry sends again
with the same `Idempotency-Key`, because the key comes from the job's input and not from the attempt,
and the receiver deduplicates on it. That is the at-least-once contract working: an effect can repeat
only under its own key.

## Do this, not that

| Instead of | Do | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| static/instance fields for progress | `SetVariableAsync` / `GetVariableOrDefaultAsync` | fields die with the process; variables are rows |
| `Task.Delay` or `Thread.Sleep` | `await ctx.SleepAsync("cool-down", delay, ct: ct)` | delays hold a worker; durable sleep frees it and survives deploys |
| calling an API directly in the body | `await ctx.RunStepAsync("charge", ct => ...)` | a step records its outcome, so a retry does not repeat recorded work |
| `catch { }` around the body | let it throw, or `await ctx.FailAsync(reason)` | swallowing turns a retryable failure into a silent success |
| polling a flag in a loop | `await ctx.TryWaitSignalAsync("approved", timeout)` | polling burns a worker; a signal parks the job, and the timeout keeps it from parking forever |
| starting children and looping until done | `await ctx.JoinAsync([audit, receipt], ct)` on the children you started (a `TimeSpan` before the token sets a deadline), or `MapAsync` when the children come from a list | the parent parks instead of occupying a worker |
| `DateTime.Now` | `DateTime.UtcNow`, or a value from the input | the ledger is UTC throughout |

## Waiting for an outside event

A handler parks on a named signal and something outside raises it: a webhook, an operator, another
job. `var r = await ctx.TryWaitSignalAsync("shipped", TimeSpan.FromDays(14), ct);` returns a
`SignalWaitOutcome`; branch on `r.TimedOut` to handle the deadline in code. The other overload,
`await ctx.WaitSignalAsync("shipped", TimeSpan.FromDays(14), ct)`, returns nothing, and a timeout
ends the job `Cancelled` with reason `wait-timed-out` instead of returning; use it only when a
missed deadline should stop the job. Both are typed too: `TryWaitSignalAsync<T>` returns
`SignalWaitOutcome<T>` with `Value`, and `WaitSignalAsync<T>` returns the raised value; the value is
null when the signal was raised without one. The raising side is
`await jobs.RaiseSignalAsync(jobRef, "shipped", new Shipped(trackingId), ct)` on `IJobs`, and an
`actor:` argument before the token names who raised it. The deadline is stored once, as
database time plus the timeout, so restarts and downtime never lengthen it, and a raise that lands
before the parked job re-enters still wins. An expired wait stays expired, through a restart too: the
restarted job reaches the same wait and is cancelled again at once, and a late raise changes nothing.
A second window is a wait under a new name (`"shipped-2"`) or a new job.

## Child jobs and fan-out

A handler starts other jobs as children and parks until they end. The parent holds no worker while it
waits, and each child is an ordinary job with its own row, retries, and steps. The first argument of
every call is a name, and the name makes the start run-once: on re-entry the same name finds the child
it already started.

| To | Call | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| run one child and wait | `await ctx.ExecuteChildAsync("email", new SendEmail(orderId), ct)` | `JobOutcome`: `Succeeded`, `Status`, `ThrowIfFailed()` |
| run one child and read its result | `await ctx.ExecuteChildAsync("label", ShippingJobs.PrintLabel(new PrintLabel(orderId)), ct)` | `JobOutcome<TResult>`: also `Value`, `ValueOrThrow()` |
| run one child per item of a list | `await ctx.MapAsync("reserve", skus, itemKey: sku => sku, child: sku => new ReserveStock(orderId, sku), ct)` | `MapOutcome<TKey>`: `Items` (each `Key` and `Outcome`), `Failed`, `ThrowIfAnyFailed()` |
| run different jobs at once | `await ctx.ParallelAsync("notify", p => p.Child("email", new SendEmail(orderId)).Child("sms", new SendSms(orderId)), ct)` | `ParallelOutcome`: `Branches["sms"]`, `Failed`, `ThrowIfAnyFailed()` |
| start now, wait later | `var audit = await ctx.StartChildAsync("audit", new Audit(orderId), ct);` then `await ctx.WaitChildAsync(audit, ct)` for one, or `await ctx.JoinAsync([audit, receipt], ct)` for several | `JobOutcome`; `ChildrenWaitOutcome`: `Children`, `Failed`, `ThrowIfAnyFailed()` |

- A failed or cancelled child never throws in the parent by itself. Every wait answers an outcome and the handler decides: `ThrowIfFailed()` or `ThrowIfAnyFailed()` to fail with it, or branch on `Failed` and compensate. A group waits for every child; it never fails fast and never cancels siblings.
- Every child ends in a `JobOutcome`, alone or as a member of a group: `JobRef`, `Status`, `Succeeded`, `TimedOut`, and `ThrowIfFailed()`. `IJobs.WaitAsync` answers the same type outside a handler.
- A child's result rides on the outcome when the child was started from the manifest's call (`ShippingJobs.PrintLabel(...)`). For a group member, read it by id: `await ctx.GetChildResultAsync<string>(item.Outcome.JobId, ct)` throws when there is none, and `TryGetChildResultAsync<T>` answers `(Found, Value)`.
- `MapAsync`, `ParallelAsync`, and `JoinAsync` take a `TimeSpan` timeout before the token: one deadline for the whole group, which cancels only the members still running and reports `TimedOut` on the outcome.
- A group does not limit how many of its children run at once; that is `ConcurrencyLimit` on the child's definition.
- The runnable proof is `concepts/200-durable-execution/215-map-parallel-join`; a failed child's outcomes are in `219-child-failure-outcomes`.

## Recurring work

`[Schedule("every-5s", "PT5S")]` on a `[Job]` makes a permanent job: one durable job the schedule
fires again and again. The job sits `Idle` between firings and holds no thread; the admission
engine makes it `Ready` when a schedule is due, a worker claims it like any job, and the handler
returns when its bounded work is done. Never loop forever inside the handler and never poll from it:
a firing that finds nothing to do returns, and the next firing comes on schedule. Acta's progress is
the schedule cursor (`next_occurrence_at_utc`); the handler's progress, such as a synchronization
watermark, is a durable variable on the job (`ctx.GetVariableOrDefaultAsync` at the top of every
execution, `ctx.SetVariableAsync` after the work it covers), carried across firings, retries, and
workers, so a recovered firing continues where the lost one stopped. Write the work first and the
variable after it, and make the work an upsert: an attempt that dies between the two replays one
batch. A definition whose occurrences are each their own job, with
their own retries, result, and retention, declares `ScheduledDelivery = ScheduledDeliveryCode.PerOccurrence`.
A finite schedule declares `StartAtUtc` and `EndBeforeUtc` (UTC with a `Z`): its occurrences fall in
[start, end) and it reads `exhausted` past the end. The runnable proof, with a killed worker, is
`concepts/100-scheduling/109-continuous-synchronization`.

## Choosing between a lane, a key, a limit, and a rate

One axis each: a lane decides ORDER, a concurrency key and its limit decide HOW MANY run at once, and a
rate decides HOW OFTEN. For one job at a time per customer, account, or aggregate, use a lane: it adds
order, and the jobs waiting behind its head cost the claim nothing, where a busy key's waiting jobs are
claimed, bounced, and re-armed. Use a bare `ConcurrencyKey` only when order must not hold work up: a
lane's failing head blocks the jobs behind it until it succeeds or exhausts MaxAttempts, and a key's
does not. Use `ConcurrencyLimit` for N at once and `RateLimit` for pacing; they combine.

## Limiting how much runs at once

`options.ConcurrencyKey("rebuild:acme")` on an enqueue admits one job of that key at a time,
cluster-wide: the runner takes the key's lease after the claim and before the handler, and a loser
re-arms Ready a couple of seconds out without spending retry budget. `[Job("rebuild-index",
ConcurrencyLimit = 4)]` sizes that gate: the key gets four concurrency slots instead of one. When an enqueue
supplies no key, the definition name is the key, so a limit alone throttles the whole definition. Two
definitions on the same key share its slots and the key's capacity is the largest limit among them.
It is mutual exclusion, never ordering: an older job can be overtaken while the key stays busy.

## Running jobs in order

`options.Lane("customer-42")` on an enqueue, or `[Job("sync-orders", Lane = "orders")]` on a
definition, puts the job in a lane: one job of the lane runs at a time, in enqueue order, like an SQS
FIFO message group. The jobs behind the head are `Blocked` until it finishes (Succeeded, Failed on
its last attempt, or Cancelled), and a failing head keeps retrying in place, holding the lane. A lane
is order, not a condition: the next job runs after a failed or cancelled head too, so a job that may
only follow a success checks for it in its first step. Rows
staged in sequence through the outbox with a lane reach it in staging order, a rejected row keeping its place. An
enqueue lane overrides the definition's. A lane is a name: ASCII dotted kebab-case up to 128 characters,
lowercased on input. Rules that bite: never enqueue a child into the lane of an unfinished ancestor (refused
at enqueue), never put a lane on a scheduled definition (refused), give waits across lanes a timeout,
and restart of a finished laned job runs that job again, right after the lane's current head.

`[Job("send-invoice", RateLimit = "10/s")]` paces how OFTEN attempts are admitted, which is a
different gate from how many run at once, and a job passes both. The value is a count per second,
minute, or hour, `N/s`, `N/m`, or `N/h`, at most 1000 a second: one every four seconds is `15/m`.
It paces admissions, not starts,
and is no hard burst cap: a turn admitted late can land beside an on-time one. Every execution takes a
turn, a retry and a resume after a wait included, so a handler that waits meets its own meter on each
re-entry: to pace one outside call inside a longer workflow, put the rate on a small child job that
makes the call. `RateName` names
the meter when several definitions should share one; omitted, the meter is the definition name.
A meter belongs to one namespace: definitions in different namespaces never share it, so a partner
quota shared by two services needs its rate split between them. Definitions on one meter must
declare the same rate. A job that arrives early is BOOKED the next free instant: under a quarter second away
the executor sleeps it out and takes it, farther away the job re-arms Ready at exactly that instant
without spending retry budget (reason `rate-limited`, never a failure and never an alert). A booked
turn stays valid for a second, or for the rate's interval when that is longer, so a backlog drains
in arrival order at the rate with one re-arm per job; a job picked up later than that is metered
again.

## Payloads

Inline payloads (inputs, step results, variables) are capped at 1 MiB (`MaxInlinePayloadBytes`).
Caller-supplied oversized writes throw `PayloadTooLargeException`; an oversized handler RESULT is
dropped while the job still succeeds, its success event carrying reason `result-oversized`, and an
oversized step result fails the job for good, since a retry would run the step again. Big artifacts
belong in blob storage with the job carrying a reference: URI, checksum, size.

By default an input with no data uses the `none` format, `byte[]`/`ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` use `bytes`, and every
other input, scalars included, is JSON (`"hello"`, `42`); an explicit or custom format overrides that. A raw or
HTTP enqueue in the json format sends strict JSON (one value, no comments or trailing commas) or is refused.

## Things that are not what they sound like

- A `Suspended` job is healthy, not stuck: it is waiting on a signal, a child, or a timer. A wait
  armed with a timeout resolves itself when the deadline passes; an unbounded wait parks until
  raised.
- An alert for a failed job is not instant. The `sys.alerts` job turns failure events into alerts once
  a minute, so one appears up to about two minutes after the failure. A handler that wants one now
  writes it: `await ctx.AlertAsync("Stock low", "Bin 7 is empty", AlertSeverityCode.Warning, ct: ct)`.
- Retention deletes finished work only. A job that landed `Succeeded`, `Failed`, or `Cancelled` is
  deleted with its steps and checkpoints once its definition's `JobRetention` has passed, 90 days by
  default (`[Job("release-payment", JobRetention = "365d")]`). A job that waits is never deleted,
  however long it waits, and a finished child stays while its parent is unfinished. Events go by age
  alone, a year by default (`JobsOptions.JobEventsRetention`): a job still waiting after that keeps
  everything it needs to resume and loses the oldest lines of its timeline. A record the business
  must keep for good belongs in the application's own table, written in a step.
- Deduplication keys keep their case (printable ASCII, no whitespace, surrounding whitespace
  trimmed): `Order-1` and `order-1` are two keys, so lowercase an id yourself when its source is
  case-insensitive.
- The enqueue `deduplicationKey` prevents a second job ROW, not a second side effect; execution
  stays at-least-once either way.
- Tags are for finding jobs, not for carrying data: input is typed and versioned, tags are
  searchable labels.
- A permanent job keeps its step results and variables from one fire to the next: a step that
  succeeded on Monday returns Monday's result on Tuesday. Put the period in the step name
  (`$"invoice-{period}"`), or call `ctx.ResetStateAsync` as the handler's last action so the next fire
  starts clean. Never at the top: a reset there also runs on every retry and replay of the same fire,
  erasing its own progress, so succeeded steps run again and an `AtMostOnce` body can run twice.
- Children a permanent job starts are never purged while its schedule lives, since retention keeps a
  child as long as its parent is unfinished. For per-occurrence fan-out, declare the definition
  `ScheduledDelivery = ScheduledDeliveryCode.PerOccurrence`: each occurrence is then a root job of its
  own, and the children it starts drain with it.

## Watch a job

Every Acta host is also a control CLI: `<app> jobs <verb>` runs against the app's own configured database
and exits, starting no worker, so it must run with the same configuration and environment as the app.
Keep the job ref an enqueue returns (`job_...`); it is the job's public identity everywhere.

```bash
dotnet run --no-build -v q -- jobs status  <job-ref> --json   # {"jobRef":"job_...","status":"succeeded"}
dotnet run --no-build -v q -- jobs explain <job-ref> --json   # what happened and what to do next
dotnet run --no-build -v q -- jobs events  <job-ref> --json   # the timeline, newest first, --take <n> to bound it
```

- `-v q` keeps `dotnet run`'s own `Using launch settings from ...` line off stdout, so `--json` output pipes into `jq`; the launch profile, and with it the environment, still applies.
- `explain` first for anything stuck, waiting, or failed: one read of the status, lease, worker, newest
  steps, checkpoints, and latest reason, with a headline and the next actions.
- Exit codes: 0 found or applied, 1 rejected or failed, 2 job not found, 64 usage error, 130 cancelled.
- `status`, `info`, `result`, `explain`, and `events` read. `cancel`, `pause`, `resume`, `restart`,
  `signal`, `debug` (runs the handler in this process), `deploy`, and `migrate` change things.
- A `ready` job with a future due instant, or a `suspended` one, is healthy: it is waiting for its
  time or its signal, and `explain` names what it waits for. A caller's wait timeout stops only the
  wait; the job keeps running.
- The dashboard at `/acta` shows the same job, and `GET /acta/api/v1/jobs/{jobRef}` answers it as JSON.

## Show jobs on your own screen

An app reads Acta through the services `UseActa` registers. Inject them like any other service.

- One job is `IJobs`. `GetAsync(jobRef)` answers the status, `NextRunAtUtc`, the lease, the parent, and the lane, or null when there is no such job. `GetStatusAsync`, `GetInputAsync`, `GetResultAsync<T>`, and `ExplainAsync` read one part. `var order = await jobs.GetInputAsync<ShipOrder>(jobRef, ct)` reads the input, as enqueued or last amended, as its type, and throws when no job matches. `ListStepsAsync(new ListJobStepsQuery(jobRef))` and `ListCheckpointsAsync(new ListJobCheckpointsQuery(jobRef))` list what the handler recorded.
- Many jobs are `IActaOperations`. `acta.Ledger.ListJobsAsync(new ListJobsQuery(JobNamespace: "shipping", Status: JobStatusCode.Failed))` finds jobs, also by `JobName`, `ParentJobId`, `CorrelationKey`, `Tags`, and `Lane`. `acta.Ledger.ListEventsAsync(new ListEventsQuery(JobId: job.JobId))` reads a timeline. `Definitions`, `Schedules`, `Alerts`, and `Workers` sit beside `Ledger`.
- A list answers a page: `Items`, `HasMore`, and `NextCursor`, which goes back in as the query's `Cursor`.
- A step shows `Name`, `Status`, `CreatedAtUtc`, and `ModifiedAtUtc`. Its result stays inside the job. A value the screen needs goes in a variable, `await ctx.SetVariableAsync("stage", new Stage("packed", 3), ct)`, and the screen reads it with `await jobs.GetVariableOrDefaultAsync<Stage>(jobRef, "stage", ct)`, null until the handler has set it. `ctx.SetProgressAsync(value, ct)` keeps one "how far along" value, last write wins, as the checkpoint `sys.progress`, which Acta's dashboard lists with the job's checkpoints; a value your own screen reads goes in a variable, as above.
- The checkpoints also list what the job waits for: a `Signal` or a `Timer` with its `DueAtUtc`, and a `ChildLatch` per child.
- A job between attempts reads `ready` with `FailureCount` above zero and its next attempt at `NextRunAtUtc`, and the step that threw reads `pending`. The exception's message is on the timeline, as the `Message` of each event whose `EventCode` is `EventCode.JobExecutionFailed`; an event also shows `CreatedAtUtc`, `DetailsText`, and `Actor`. A step's `FailureMessage` is set only for an at-most-once step that failed or was interrupted.
- Stored JSON has camelCase property names: `OrderId` is `orderId`.
- The text of a status or a kind is `.Code`: `job.Status.Code` is `suspended`, the text the CLI, the HTTP API, and SQL show, where `ToString()` gives the C# name `Suspended`. `JobStatusCodeExtensions.FromCode("suspended")` reads it back.
- Each read is its own snapshot, so two reads a moment apart can disagree while a job moves. A sleeping job reads `ready` with a future `NextRunAtUtc`; a job waiting for a signal or a child reads `suspended`.
- `jobs.GetLineageMapAsync(jobRef)` answers one job with its `Ancestors` and its direct `Children`, each list capped and flagged (`ChildrenHasMore`). It is the neighbourhood of that job, not the whole tree: walk down by asking again for a child.
- `executing` means claimed, and the concurrency slot and the rate turn are taken after the claim. A count of `executing` jobs can therefore read above a `ConcurrencyLimit` for a moment; to show what is inside a gate, show the step the handler has reached.
- A page's script can call the same reads as JSON under `/acta/api/v1`, and a link to a job in Acta's dashboard is `/acta/#/jobs/{jobRef}`.

## The HTTP API

`Acta.AspNetCore` serves Acta's operations over HTTP: `MapActaApi` maps the API alone, and `MapActa` from `Acta.Dashboard` maps it under `{pattern}/api/v1` beside the dashboard. Its contract is the OpenAPI document `docs/reference/openapi.json` in the repository. Generate a client from that document with standard OpenAPI tools; Acta ships no client package.

## When you are unsure

Every pattern above exists as a compiled, runnable example under `concepts/` in the repository:
numbered rungs from fundamentals to chaos recovery, each a small project for one idea, its program one
file named after the folder: `concepts/200-durable-execution/215-map-parallel-join/map-parallel-join.cs`. The demo apps under
`demos/` are complete deployable applications built only from the published packages. The one
complete walk from enqueue to the first test, on the consumer packages, is `docs/first-job.md`; the
rest of the `docs/` tree is indexed by task in `docs/README.md`. Start at useacta.net.
